Secret Closet
SEE-krit KLOZ-it
n. phrase (practical theology and spiritual discipline; the private place of prayer commanded by Jesus in Matthew 6:6, where the believer meets with the Father in secret, away from the audience of men)
Secret from Latin secretus, past participle of secernere (to separate, set apart), from se- (apart) + cernere (to sift, separate). Closet from Old French closet (small enclosure), diminutive of clos (enclosure), from Latin clausum (closed place). Jesus' command in Matthew 6:6 uses the Greek tameion — a storeroom, inner room, a private chamber separated from public traffic. The “secret closet” is thus a closed, private space where the soul meets God without the contaminating motive of being seen by men.

Biblical Definition

The secret closet is the space of private, hidden prayer commanded by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount: “When you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matt 6:6). The command does not abolish public or corporate prayer; it diagnoses the motive that poisons it: the desire to be seen and admired by men (Matt 6:5). The secret closet removes that motive by removing the audience; only the Father remains, and He “sees in secret.” The promise of the secret closet is reciprocal: the God who sees in secret rewards openly. Psalm 91:1 provides the Old Testament parallel: “He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.” The “secret place” is the place of covenant intimacy. Daniel 6:10 is the supreme Old Testament example: Daniel, under threat of death, continued his practice of three-times-daily prayer in his upper room with his windows open toward Jerusalem — the secret closet maintained under the fiercest pressure. Mark 1:35 shows Jesus modeling the discipline: “in the morning, while it was still very dark, He arose and went out and departed to a deserted place — and there He prayed.” The Son of God did not assume intimacy with the Father; He pursued it, early and privately. The Puritans enshrined the secret closet as the indispensable center of all vital piety.

Webster 1828 Definition

The private, hidden place and practice of prayer commanded by Jesus in Matthew 6:6, where the believer meets the Father without the audience of men and receives from the God who “sees in secret” — the indispensable center of personal piety in the Puritan-Reformed tradition.

SECRET CLOSET, n. phrase. The private place and practice of prayer commanded by Christ in Matthew 6:6: a closed room, separated from public view, where the believer kneels before the Father who “sees in secret” and promises to “reward openly.” The command arises in direct contrast to the hypocrite who prays on street corners to be seen by men (Matt 6:5) — the secret closet removes the false audience and leaves only the real one.

The Greek tameion (Matt 6:6) denotes a private inner room, a storeroom apart from the main chambers — not a specific architectural requirement but a principle of hiddenness. The principle is: go where men cannot see you, shut the door behind you, and address the invisible God who is nonetheless present and attentive. The public/private distinction in prayer is not about the legitimacy of corporate worship; Jesus Himself prayed with His disciples (Luke 11:1) and at public gatherings (John 11:41–42). The secret closet targets the motive: prayer that craves human admiration has already received its reward (Matt 6:5); prayer that seeks the Father receives the Father's reward.

The Puritan tradition elevated the secret closet to the standard of genuine Christianity. Matthew Henry's A Method for Prayer (1710) structured the content of the secret closet in detail: adoration, confession, petition, intercession, and thanksgiving, each with a treasury of biblical language to fill the hour. Richard Baxter insisted that a pastor who neglects his secret closet has nothing to give his congregation. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) assumed that private prayer was the bedrock on which public worship rested.

Psalm 91:1 provides the Old Testament theology of the secret closet: “He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.” The “secret place” (seter, hiddenness, shelter) names the intimate covenant space where God's presence is known most directly — a place entered not by genealogy or church attendance but by deliberate, personal approach. Daniel 6:10 enacts the discipline under maximum pressure: the decree against prayer did not alter Daniel's three-times-daily practice; it only confirmed it.

Mark 1:35 is the Christological anchor of the secret closet: the Son of God, whose public ministry was unparalleled in power and fruitfulness, still departed early and alone to pray in a deserted place. If the Incarnate Son pursued the secret closet, the believing sinner cannot claim exemption. The discipline is not optional; it is modeled from the top.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:6 — "But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you."

Psalm 91:1 — "He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."

Daniel 6:10 — "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went home. And in his upper room, with his windows open toward Jerusalem, he knelt down on his knees three times that day, and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as was his custom since early days."

Mark 1:35 — "And in the morning, while it was still very dark, He arose and went out and departed to a deserted place — and there He prayed."

Modern Corruption

Social media Christianity broadcasts prayers that belong in the closet, converting private devotion into public performance; the busyness of modern ministry and family life chronically displaces the secret closet rather than organizing around it.

expand to see more

Matthew 6:5 named the hypocrite who “loves to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners so that they may be seen by men.” Social media has constructed an infinite street corner: the online prayer request, the public devotional post, the Instagram quiet time, and the live-streamed morning prayer all carry, to greater or lesser degree, the structural temptation to perform for an audience. This is not to say that sharing Scripture publicly is sin — there is a legitimate witness function — but when the public post replaces the private closet, or when the motivation for public prayer is audience rather than God, the reward Jesus warns of has been received in full: the approval of men, who have seen it, and no reward from the Father. The diagnostic question is simple: would you still pray if no one would know?

The pastoral disease of busyness — filling ministry hours with counseling, administration, sermon preparation, and meetings — has historically been the secret closet's primary assassin. Richard Baxter's complaint in The Reformed Pastor (1656) is as current as the day it was written: ministers neglect their own souls in the effort to tend others' souls, and the congregation suffers accordingly. A pastor who has not met God in his private chamber before entering his pulpit has nothing to give but his own opinions — however carefully prepared. The secret closet is not one item in a devotional checklist; it is the spring that feeds every other stream of ministry. When it runs dry, everything downstream dries with it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The secret closet is rooted in Jesus' Sermon on the Mount command (Matt 6:6), modeled in His own pre-dawn prayer practice (Mark 1:35), enacted by Daniel in the Old Testament (Dan 6:10), developed extensively in Puritan practical theology, and enshrined in the Reformed tradition's account of personal piety.

expand to see more

Matthew 6:5–8 (Sermon on the Mount) — the foundational command; set in contrast to hypocritical public prayer (v. 5) and pagan vain repetition (v. 7); the secret closet is defined by the motive (pleasing the Father alone), not by the architecture.

Mark 1:35 — the Christological model; Jesus rises before dawn, departs to solitude, and prays — establishing that the pattern of private retreat to the Father is not a concession to weakness but a discipline practiced by the Son Himself.

Daniel 6:10 — the Old Testament paradigm; Daniel's thrice-daily secret-closet practice maintained under the death decree; the political pressure did not alter the devotional pattern, demonstrating that the secret closet is not a fair-weather discipline.

Matthew Henry, A Method for Prayer (1710) — the most comprehensive Puritan guide to secret-closet content; structures adoration, confession, petition, intercession, and thanksgiving with scriptural language for each; remains the finest practical manual for filling the secret closet with the Word.

1689 LBCF, Chapter 22 (Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day) — §6: “Prayer with thanksgiving, being one part of natural worship, is by God required of all men”; the confession identifies prayer as an obligation of the natural order, not merely a spiritual gift, grounding the secret closet in creation as well as redemption.

Usage

"The diagnostic for a living versus a dead prayer life is often the secret closet: a believer who prays publicly but rarely privately has learned to perform for an audience; a believer who meets God regularly in the private room will find that public prayer flows naturally from what was already said between them."

"Daniel's secret closet (Dan 6:10) was maintained with his windows open toward Jerusalem — directional prayer, geographically oriented to the covenant promise; this suggests that the secret closet need not be interior or passive but can be structured, directional, and informed by the promises of Scripture."

"Mark 1:35 should govern a minister's morning schedule: Jesus rose “while it was still very dark” to pray before the crowds arrived; a minister who allows the demands of others to crowd out his secret closet has reversed the order Christ established — the crowd's need was real, and Jesus met it, but only after He had first met the Father."
